questions.question: What does a polynomial commitment scheme like KZG let a prover do after publishing a commitment C?
options: Prove statements about f(z) at chosen points without revealing all coefficients of f
Encrypt the polynomial so nobody can evaluate it at any point
Compress the polynomial into fewer coefficients with no loss
Turn any polynomial into a hash function with collision resistance
questions.explanation: A polynomial commitment binds to f and enables short evaluation proofs at specific points z.

questions.question: In KZG, which value is considered the 'toxic waste' that must be destroyed after setup?
options: The secret scalar s used to generate the SRS powers [s^i]
The public SRS list of group elements [s^i]
The verifier’s chosen evaluation point z
The polynomial coefficients a_i
questions.explanation: If s is known, an attacker can break binding by forging openings; the SRS is meant to be public.

questions.question: In additive notation, what is the KZG commitment to f(x)=Σ a_i x^i given an SRS containing [s^i] in G1?
options: C = Σ a_i · [s^i] = [f(s)]
C = [Σ a_i] (sum of coefficients only)
C = [f(z)] for the verifier’s chosen z
C = Σ [a_i] · s^i (scalars outside the group)
questions.explanation: The commitment is a linear combination of SRS powers, which equals [f(s)] at the secret setup point.

questions.question: What is the witness (quotient) polynomial used for a single-point opening at z?
options: q(x) = f(x) · (x - z)
q(x) = f(z) / (x - z)
q(x) = f(x) - z
questions.explanation: Dividing by (x - z) removes the root at z, producing a polynomial q such that f(x)-f(z)=(x-z)q(x).

questions.question: Which theorem explains why dividing f(x) by (x - z) leaves remainder f(z)?
options: Remainder theorem
Chinese remainder theorem
Fermat’s little theorem
Cayley–Hamilton theorem
questions.explanation: The remainder theorem states that the remainder of division by (x - z) is exactly f(z).

questions.question: Which pairing equation is the core KZG verification check in additive notation?
questions.explanation: It enforces f(s)-y = q(s)(s-z) in the exponent without revealing s, using C=[f(s)] and π=[q(s)].

questions.question: Attack scenario: if an adversary learns the toxic waste s after the ceremony, what can they do?
options: Forge valid-looking openings for commitments, breaking binding
Make the pairing bilinear again so verification starts working
Prevent anyone from computing commitments from coefficients
Convert the scheme into an information-theoretic commitment
questions.explanation: Knowing s lets the adversary manipulate witnesses/openings and produce proofs for false evaluations.

questions.question: If a prover tries to commit to a polynomial whose degree exceeds the setup's max_degree, what should a correct implementation do?
options: Reject (or fail) because the SRS does not cover the needed powers
Automatically truncate higher-degree coefficients to fit
Accept, because KZG verification is constant-size anyway
Replace missing SRS powers with zeros and accept
questions.explanation: The SRS only includes [s^i] up to max_degree; exceeding it makes the commitment undefined and must be rejected.
